items.prompt: Which term describes teams reinventing a button because no shared system exists yet?
choices: Design debt
Visual drift
Orphaned component
Governance decay
items.explanation: Drift is what happens before a shared source of truth exists.

items.prompt: What does design debt describe?
choices: A budget shortfall in the design department
The cost of buying design software licenses
Exceptions accumulating inside an existing system
Unfinished mockups left in a designer's drafts
items.explanation: Debt is built up from deliberate departures inside a system that already exists.

items.prompt: What is an orphaned component?
choices: A component whose designer left the company
A component with no visual states defined
A component used on exactly one screen
A library component almost nothing still uses
items.explanation: An orphan is defined by lack of use, not by who made it.

items.prompt: When does design debt usually show up?
choices: Years into a mature system under deadlines
On the day the first button is designed
Only when a system has fewer than ten components
Only after a full visual rebrand
items.explanation: Debt needs time and sustained deadlines to accumulate.

items.prompt: Why is the word 'debt' used?
choices: Every exception needs a formal loan approval
Exceptions buy speed now and cost confusion later
Designers are paid per component they create
The system's license fees grow each year
items.explanation: Like a loan, an exception pays out immediately and charges interest later.

items.prompt: Does design debt mean the system failed?
choices: Yes; a working system never has any exceptions
Yes; it proves the original spec was wrong
No; most long-lived systems gather some
Only if more than one squad is involved
items.explanation: Some debt is normal. What matters is whether anyone repays it.

items.prompt: A spec lists 3 buttons and the codebase has 37. How many are outside the spec?
items.explanation: 37 minus the 3 in the spec leaves 34.

items.prompt: Which situation is visual drift rather than design debt?
choices: Two squads build different buttons with no system yet
A taller button added to a mature system for one banner
A leftover card nobody in a mature system still uses
A local copy of a library button never merged back
items.explanation: The other three all happen inside an existing system.

items.prompt: An engineer copies a library button into a local file and tweaks it, three years after the system launched. Drift or debt?
choices: Drift; any inconsistency counts as drift whatever the system's age
Drift; the copy was made by an individual, not a team
Debt; a deliberate departure from a system that already exists
Neither; a single tweaked button is too small to count
items.explanation: A system exists, and the copy bypasses it on purpose: that is debt. Size and who did it do not change the category.
items.reference:
Drift versus debt
🌱 drift: no shared system yet, teams reinvent
🏗️ debt: system exists, exceptions pile up inside it
👻 orphan: a component almost nothing uses
Why: the presence of an existing source of truth separates the two.
items.learnMore:
Debt lives inside the system

Drift is the problem a design system solves. Debt is what happens to a system that already works: each exception buys speed now and costs confusion later, and it stays unpaid unless someone is scheduled to repay it.

Common mistake

Treating any inconsistency as drift, and so expecting the system itself to fix it.
items.reflection: Think of a shared drawer at home or work that started tidy. Which mess came from having no system, and which from exceptions piling up inside one?

items.prompt: Three squads with no shared library each build a different card component. What is this, and what addresses its cause?
choices: Debt; a quarterly audit of every card variant
Drift; a stricter review of each squad's cards
Debt; deleting the two least used card variants
Drift; a shared system with one source of truth
items.explanation: With no system there is nothing to be in debt to. The cause is the missing source of truth, so that is what fixes it.

Inconsistency comes only from teams with no system

items.prompt: Which of these is one of the four ways debt accumulates?
choices: Token renaming
Contrast checking
Silent forking
Dark mode support
items.explanation: The four are unreconciled one-offs, orphans, governance decay and silent forking.

items.prompt: A component built for a campaign outlives it because nobody owns removal. Which mechanism?
choices: Governance decay
Silent forking
A token naming clash
An unreconciled one-off
items.explanation: A one-off with no removal owner stays after its purpose ends.

items.prompt: What is silent forking?
choices: Copying a component locally and never merging it back
Splitting a design file into two branches on purpose
Renaming a component without telling the team
Deleting a component that is still being used
items.explanation: Two copies drift independently once 'later' never arrives.

items.prompt: What does governance decay mean?
choices: Reviewers get stricter as the system grows
The review step stops being enforced over time
Components slowly lose their visual polish
Tokens expire after a fixed number of years
items.explanation: The process that resolved exceptions quietly lapses.

items.prompt: Why does a leftover exception get copied?
choices: The build tool copies unused files automatically
Designers must reuse the oldest component
Searchers see it in use and assume it is approved
Copying is the documented way to handle exceptions
items.explanation: Visible use looks like approval to the next person under pressure.

items.prompt: In the debt loop, what creates the next exception?
choices: A fresh design audit
A completed adoption
A spec update
Deadline pressure
items.explanation: The loop restarts each time a deadline makes the shortcut attractive.

items.prompt: How many mechanisms does the unit list for debt accumulating?
choices: Four
Three
Five
Six
items.explanation: Unreconciled one-offs, orphans, governance decay and silent forking.

items.prompt: An orphaned component is dangerous mainly because...
choices: it slows the build for every screen
it looks like a valid option to the next searcher
it always contains a security flaw
it forces designers to learn a new tool
items.explanation: A leftover in the library reads as approved even if it fits nothing.

items.prompt: A reorg removes the team that reviewed exceptions, and nothing visibly breaks. Which mechanism is at work, and why is it dangerous?
choices: Silent forking; local copies slowly break the build
An orphan; the removed team's components crash
A one-off; the reorg itself is the exception
Governance decay; new exceptions pile up unseen
items.explanation: Exceptions keep arriving while the step that resolved them is gone. Nothing crashes, so no alarm rings.
items.reference:
Four feeders of the loop
🎯 unreconciled one-offs: no owner for removal
👻 orphans: shipped features replaced them
🕳️ governance decay: the review step lapses
🍴 silent forking: a local copy never merges back
Why: each mechanism keeps an exception alive after its reason is gone.
items.learnMore:
The loop, not a single failure

Deadline pressure creates an exception, review rarely resolves it, it becomes precedent, and the next deadline copies it. The four mechanisms are the ways an exception avoids ever being resolved.

Common mistake

Hunting for the one decision that broke the system when the cause is the loop.
items.reflection: Think of a temporary fix you have seen outlive its reason. Which of the four mechanisms kept it alive?

items.prompt: A squad copies a library card into its repo to avoid waiting for a release, planning to merge later. What is the cost?
choices: Two versions drift apart, and later rarely arrives
The library card is deleted from the shared system
The squad's card gets automatic updates it did not ask for
Nothing, since a local copy is invisible to other squads
items.explanation: This is silent forking: the copy is fast now but diverges, and reconciliation keeps getting postponed.

items.prompt: Which action most directly breaks the debt loop?
choices: A larger library with more variants to choose from
A rule that exceptions need a longer design brief
A scheduled review ending each exception in adopt or delete
A one-time cleanup of every current variant
items.explanation: The loop continues because exceptions go unresolved; a standing review forces an ending each time. A one-off cleanup does not stop new debt.

items.prompt: How many outcomes can an exception have under the test?
choices: Two
One
Three
Four
items.explanation: Adopt or delete; 'leave it' is not an outcome.

items.prompt: What does 'adopt' give an exception?
choices: A longer deadline for its eventual removal
Tokens, a spec, an owner and documentation
A private copy in each squad's code
A lower priority in the next audit queue
items.explanation: Adopting makes it a first-class component.

items.prompt: What does 'delete' involve?
choices: Hiding it from the documentation and the search index
Freezing it so nobody can edit it
Moving usages back to the existing component
Renaming it with a legacy prefix
items.explanation: Delete means the usages are actually moved, not just hidden.

items.prompt: Does a high usage count justify adopting an exception?
choices: Yes; popular components are always well designed
Yes; removing them always costs more
Only if three or more squads use it
No; it only shows the decision is overdue
items.explanation: Unreviewed components are copied just like reviewed ones.

items.prompt: If an exception fails any one of the three questions, what happens?
choices: It is deleted
It is adopted
It is frozen
It is forked
items.explanation: Only three yes answers lead to adopt.

items.prompt: Which question asks whether the difference is deliberate?
choices: Does it solve a recurring, distinct need?
Is the difference intentional, not drift?
Does formalizing cost less than the confusion?
Is its owner still on the team?
items.explanation: The second question separates deliberate design from sloppiness.

items.prompt: Is 'leave it as is' a valid outcome?
choices: Yes, whenever the exception looks small enough
Yes, once a year at most
No; leaving it undecided is how it spreads
Yes, if its usage stays stable
items.explanation: The nine-screen spread came from leaving it.

items.prompt: How many of the three answers must be yes to adopt?
choices: At least one
Any two
Only the first
All three
items.explanation: A single no sends the exception to delete.

items.prompt: A card solves a real recurring need, but its difference from the standard card is just sloppy padding. What is the result?
choices: Adopt; the need is real, so the padding can be fixed later
Delete; the difference is accidental, so usages move back
Adopt; the card already has screens that rely on it
Leave it; accidental differences are too small to matter
items.explanation: It fails the second question. Accidental drift is not a reason for a separate component.
items.reference:
The test
1️⃣ real, recurring, distinct need?
2️⃣ difference intentional, not drift?
3️⃣ formalizing cheaper than the confusion?
✅ all yes: adopt ❌ any no: delete
Why: leaving an exception undecided is what lets it spread.
items.learnMore:
Two endings, no third

Adopt gives the exception tokens, a spec, an owner and docs. Delete migrates its usages back to the existing component. A high usage count is not a vote for adopting; it only shows the decision is overdue.

Common mistake

Reading nine screens of usage as proof the exception is good.
items.reflection: Think of a workaround in your own work that became permanent. Which of the three questions would it have failed?

items.prompt: A variant on 12 screens meets a real need, differs on purpose, and needs one day to formalize. What is the result?
choices: Delete; twelve screens is already too much spread to keep safely
Wait a full quarter so that more usage makes the choice clearer
Adopt; it passes all three questions whatever the screen count
Adopt only after all twelve screens have been rewritten first
items.explanation: The count is not part of the test. All three answers are yes, so it is adopted.

items.prompt: Which model has a dedicated team deciding every exception?
choices: Federated stewardship
Centralized team
Community with a gate
Informal memory
items.explanation: One team owns every decision.

items.prompt: Which model assigns one owner per product area?
choices: Centralized team
Community with a gate
Federated stewardship
Rotating volunteers
items.explanation: Stewards run the test for their own domain.

items.prompt: What does an automated gate do?
choices: Rewrites components automatically to match the spec
Reviews the visual quality of each component
Deletes unused components every night
Flags undocumented new components before merge
items.explanation: It catches exceptions at the moment they are created.

items.prompt: What is the main weakness of a centralized team?
choices: It becomes a bottleneck as the org grows
Its decisions differ across product areas
It has no clear owner for decisions
It cannot be defended in a budget review
items.explanation: A fixed team cannot scale with exception volume.

items.prompt: What is the main weakness of federated stewardship?
choices: One reorg removes every reviewer at once
Stewards drift apart without a shared forum
Exceptions are caught only months later
It needs a custom lint rule to work
items.explanation: Without a shared forum, areas decide differently.

items.prompt: What is the main weakness of an automated gate?
choices: It reviews only after the release ships
It needs every squad to attend a meeting
It catches code, not design judgment
It cannot run on new components
items.explanation: A rule can detect a missing spec but not judge the need.

items.prompt: Does any governance model remove the need for the test?
choices: Yes; the automated gate replaces it entirely
Yes; having stewards makes it unnecessary
Yes, once the library is large
No; models only change who runs it and when
items.explanation: The decision still has to be made.

items.prompt: Which model best survives a single reorg?
choices: Federated stewardship
A centralized team
A single lead designer
Informal memory
items.explanation: Spreading ownership means one cut does not remove it all.

items.prompt: Three product areas each adopt a slightly different compact card. Which model and failure is this?
choices: Centralized with a bottleneck; the team adopted too slowly
A gate with no judgment; it approved every card
Federated with no shared forum; drift returns one layer up
Community review; nobody proposed a card
items.explanation: Stewards without a shared forum decide independently, so the same need gets three answers.
items.reference:
Three models
🏢 centralized: one team decides, bottlenecks as the org grows
🧭 federated: one steward per area, drifts without a forum
🤖 gate: CI flags new components, catches code not judgment
Why: each model changes who runs the test and when; none removes it.
items.learnMore:
Pick by failure mode

Each model trades differently: the centralized team is consistent but a bottleneck, federated stewards scale but drift apart, a gate catches exceptions early but cannot judge them. Pairings cover each other's weaknesses.

Common mistake

Choosing a model as if it removed the need for the adopt-or-delete test.

items.explanation: A rigid rule with no sanctioned way to ship a temporary exception pushes people around it.

items.prompt: Which check finds components that nothing uses?
choices: A scheduled usage audit
The adopt-or-delete test
A visual regression test
A color contrast check
items.explanation: The audit looks at existing components, not new ones.

items.prompt: What does the adopt-or-delete test run on?
choices: Every component nightly
New exceptions as they appear
Only already-deleted components
Only color tokens
items.explanation: It reviews arrivals, not slow decay.

items.prompt: What does the audit ask about each library component?
choices: Was it designed by the original team?
Is its name shorter than ten letters?
Is anything shipping still using it?
Does it have more than three variants?
items.explanation: Usage is the signal for an orphan.

items.prompt: Can an approved, documented component become an orphan?
choices: No; a spec and owner protect it from going unused
No; owners are assigned for life
Only if its tokens change
Yes; when the feature it served is redesigned
items.explanation: Approval says nothing about future use.

items.prompt: Who should retire an orphan?
choices: A named owner assigned by the audit
Whoever notices it first, informally
The newest designer by default
Nobody, since orphans are harmless
items.explanation: Without a named owner, retirement does not happen.

items.prompt: Why does the first test miss orphans?
choices: It only checks color tokens in the shared library
It looks at new exceptions, not old unused ones
It runs once at launch and then stops
It deletes components before they are used
items.explanation: Orphans form without any new exception appearing.

items.prompt: How often should the usage audit run?
choices: Only after an incident has already happened
Never, since code review covers it
On a schedule, apart from new reviews
Only when a full rebrand is about to start
items.explanation: The audit is a separate recurring job.

items.prompt: What does an orphan look like to a developer searching the library?
choices: An obvious warning to avoid
A hidden file they cannot find
A deprecated token alias
A valid, approved option
items.explanation: Nothing marks it as unused, so it reads as safe to use.

items.prompt: A card was approved with a spec and owner five years ago. The feature was redesigned and nothing uses it now. Which check catches it?
choices: The adopt-or-delete test on new exceptions
The scheduled audit of component usage
The CI gate that flags missing specs
The owner's own memory of the card
items.explanation: The card is not a new exception and has a spec, so only a usage audit notices it went quiet.
items.reference:
Two checks, two jobs
🆕 adopt-or-delete: runs on each new exception
🔍 usage audit: runs on every component, on a schedule
👻 orphan: approved once, unused now
Why: the first check never looks at old components going quiet.
items.learnMore:
Approval does not last forever

A component can be adopted correctly and still become an orphan when the feature it served is redesigned. Only a scheduled usage audit asks, for every library component, whether anything still uses it.

Common mistake

Assuming that a spec and an owner mean a component is still needed.
items.reflection: Think of a cupboard you cleaned once. Why does it fill up with unused things again unless you check it regularly?

items.prompt: An audit finds a component with zero imports, but it has a spec and an owner. What is the correct response?
choices: Keep it for good, because it has an approved spec and owner
Adopt it again with a fresh spec and a new owner
Confirm zero references, then have the owner retire it
Wait until a squad asks for it, then restore the usage
items.explanation: A spec records that it was once approved, not that it is needed. Retirement is the owner's job.
items.reference:
Two checks, two jobs
🆕 adopt-or-delete: runs on each new exception
🔍 usage audit: runs on every component, on a schedule
👻 orphan: approved once, unused now

items.prompt: In the model, what share of exceptions were resolved within 30 days in year one?
items.explanation: Year one is the 88% starting point.

items.prompt: Year one has 40 screens and 3 reviewers. About how many screens each?
items.explanation: 40 divided by 3 is about 13.

items.prompt: Year three has 340 screens and 3 reviewers. About how many screens each?
items.explanation: 340 divided by 3 is about 113.

items.prompt: What does a review backlog behave like?
choices: A faster review for the oldest items
No governance for everything waiting in it
A pause that fixes itself over time
A sign reviewers are being too strict
items.explanation: Waiting exceptions can be found and copied unreviewed.

items.prompt: What changed between year one and year three?
choices: The process; reviewers got lazier
The tooling; the old one broke
The load; the process itself stayed the same
The spec; it grew too long
items.explanation: Same team, same method, far more screens.

items.prompt: What share did the model give in year three?
items.explanation: At about 113 screens per reviewer the model gives 41%.

items.prompt: Without governance, the model adds about how many orphans per year?
items.explanation: With governance it is about 2, without about 11.

items.prompt: With governance at 2 orphans a year, about how many after 36 months?
items.explanation: Three years at 2 per year is 6.

items.prompt: Using the model, how many orphans after an 18-month gap with no governance?
choices: About 11
About 22
About 3
About 17
items.explanation: 1.5 years times 11 per year is 16.5, rounded to 17. With governance it would have been about 3.
items.reference:
Review load (illustrative model)
📊 year 1: 40 screens / 3 reviewers = about 13 each, 88% resolved in 30 days
📊 year 3: 340 screens / 3 reviewers = about 113 each, 41%
⏳ backlog = no governance for whatever waits
Why: the process stayed the same; the load per reviewer grew.
items.learnMore:
Capacity must track growth

The demo fits a straight line through two points: 88% at about 13 screens per reviewer and 41% at about 113. It also models about 2 new orphans a year with governance and 11 without. These are model outputs from the unit, not measurements.

Common mistake

Reading a straight-line fit through two points as an exact law.

items.prompt: What was the first step of Northwind's remediation?
choices: Delete all orphans at once
Hire a new central team
Rewrite the spec
Inventory by real usage
items.explanation: Triage without an inventory repeats the failed informal process.

items.prompt: Why use a scripted search of imports instead of the spec?
choices: The spec was known to be stale
Scripts are faster to print
The spec forbids searching
Designers dislike reading specs
items.explanation: Real usage shows what is truly shipping.

items.prompt: 61 zero-usage orphans plus 34 used-but-undocumented components need a decision. How many in total?
items.explanation: 61 plus 34 is 95.

items.prompt: What was triaged first?
choices: Components in discovery order
Components in alphabetical order
High-usage and user-facing risks
The easiest items first
items.explanation: Risk matters more than harmless orphans.

items.prompt: What happened to the true zero-usage orphans?
choices: They were adopted with specs and owners
They were hidden from search results only
They were moved to a new library
They were deleted in one batched cleanup
items.explanation: Each was confirmed to have no remaining references first.

items.prompt: What did the CI gate flag?
choices: New components with no linked spec
Components with too many variants
Components older than a year
Components used by one squad
items.explanation: A missing spec is the signal the gate checks.

items.prompt: Why not return to one team of three?
choices: Three people would cost the company too much each year
The same capacity mismatch would recur as the product grew
Central teams are not allowed under the new org chart
Three people cannot read every spec on the roadmap
items.explanation: The cause was load per reviewer.

items.prompt: What does the monthly forum do?
choices: It assigns blame for each incident
It votes to delete the oldest components
Stewards reconcile drift between product areas
It replaces the CI gate
items.explanation: A shared forum stops areas diverging.

items.prompt: Triage choice: a harmless zero-usage orphan or a widely reused component built on wrong assumptions. Which first?
choices: The widely reused one, because its risk is active
The orphan, because deleting it is quickest
The orphan, because it is older
Neither, until every item is inventoried again
items.explanation: The reused component can harm users now, while the orphan harms no one.
items.reference:
The playbook order
1️⃣ inventory by real usage (61 + 34 = 95 need a decision)
2️⃣ triage by usage and user-facing risk
3️⃣ rebuild governance: stewards + CI gate + forum
🚦 gate allows a dated temporary-exception flag
Why: triage without an inventory repeats the informal process that failed.
items.learnMore:
Size governance to the org

Northwind rejected a return to three people because the same 113-screens-per-reviewer mismatch would recur. A gate with a dated exception flag lets deadline work ship while leaving a record the forum can act on.

Common mistake

Fixing the backlog once without resizing governance, so the backlog returns.
items.reflection: Think of cleaning a very full garage. Why does a full inventory help before deciding what to keep or throw out?

items.prompt: A team proposes triaging in discovery order to start fast. What is the problem?

A harmless orphan could be handled before a live risk
Discovery order forbids deleting anything
It makes the CI gate stop working
items.explanation: Order should follow usage and risk, not the order items happened to be found.
